facts.text: On 6 February 1998 the applicant was transferred from a police station inside the airport to the Aliens Department of the Istanbul Security Directorate. concepts.interpretation: Article 3 prohibits torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment; the Court found a violation due to risk of stoning and flogging if deported to Iran.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

concepts.interpretation: Article 13 requires an effective domestic remedy to challenge violations of Convention rights; the Court found a violation due to lack of effective remedy to challenge deportation.

anchor.surface_text: the right to political asylum is not contained in either the Convention or its Protocols (see the Vilvarajah and Others v. the United Kingdom judgment of 30 October 1991, Series A no. 215, p. 34, § 102). However, it is well established in the case-law of the Court that expulsion by a Contracting State may give rise to an issue under Article 3, and hence engage the responsibility of that State under the Convention, where substantial grounds have been shown for believing that the person in question, if expelled, would face a real risk of being subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 in the receiving country.

concepts.interpretation: States have discretion in controlling entry and expulsion but must not expel persons facing real risk of Article 3 treatment.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 implies the obligation not to expel the person in question to that country (see the Soering v. the United Kingdom judgment of 7 July 1989, Series A no. 161, pp. 35-36, §§ 90-91; the Cruz Varas and Others v. Sweden judgment of 20 March 1991, Series A no. 201, p. 28, §§ 69-70; and the Chahal v. the United Kingdom judgment of 15 November 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V, p. 1853, §§ 73-74).

concepts.interpretation: Article 3 imposes a positive obligation on States not to deport persons to a real risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment.

anchor.surface_text: a rigorous scrutiny must necessarily be conducted of an individual’s claim that his or her deportation to a third country will expose that individual to treatment prohibited by Article 3 (see, mutatis mutandis, the Chahal judgment cited above, p. 1855, § 79, and p. 1859, § 96).

concepts.interpretation: The Court applies rigorous scrutiny to claims of risk under Article 3 before deportation is allowed.

anchor.surface_text: The Court is not persuaded that the authorities of the respondent State conducted any meaningful assessment of the applicant’s claim, including its arguability. It would appear that the applicant’s failure to comply with the five-day registration requirement under the Asylum Regulation 1994 denied her any scrutiny of the factual basis of her fears about being removed to Iran (see paragraph 16 above).

concepts.interpretation: The Court found that domestic remedies were ineffective as the applicant was denied substantive assessment due to procedural time limits.

anchor.surface_text: the applicant must be considered to have had more than an arguable claim that she would be at risk if removed to her country of origin.

concepts.interpretation: The Court recognized the applicant had more than an arguable claim of risk under Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: The Court recalls that Article 13 guarantees the availability at national level of a remedy to enforce the substance of the Convention rights and freedoms in whatever form they might happen to be secured in the domestic legal order. The effect of this Article is thus to require the provision of a domestic remedy allowing the competent national authority both to deal with the substance of the relevant Convention complaint and to grant appropriate relief, although Contracting States are afforded some discretion as to the manner in which they conform to their obligations under this provision.

concepts.interpretation: Article 13 requires a remedy that addresses the substance of the complaint and grants appropriate relief, including suspension of deportation if needed.

anchor.surface_text: The Ankara Administrative Court considered that the applicant’s deportation was fully in line with domestic law requirements. It would appear that, having reached that conclusion, the court felt it unnecessary to address the substance of the applicant’s complaint, even though it was arguable on the merits in view of the UNHCR’s decision to recognise her as a refugee within the meaning of the Geneva Convention.

concepts.interpretation: The Court criticized the domestic court for acting as a fourth instance by only reviewing formal legality and not the substance of the claim.

anchor.surface_text: the automatic and mechanical application of such a short time-limit for submitting an asylum application must be considered at variance with the protection of the fundamental value embodied in Article 3 of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The applicant maintained that her removal to Iran would expose her to treatment prohibited by Article 3 of the Convention, which provides: "No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found a real risk of prohibited treatment if the applicant were deported to Iran, thus accepting the claim under Article 3.

arguments.claim: The applicant stated that she had committed adultery in Iran and had to leave before criminal proceedings could be brought against her. She submitted that she would probably have been prosecuted and sentenced to a form of inhuman punishment.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the applicant's claim as substantiated by UNHCR refugee status and reports of punishments in Iran.

arguments.claim: The applicant relied on reports by Amnesty International referring to cases of women in Iran being stoned to death for adultery and stressed she was granted refugee status by the UNHCR on the ground of well-founded fear of persecution.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court gave due weight to the UNHCR's conclusion and Amnesty International reports supporting the applicant's fear.

arguments.claim: The applicant claimed that stoning to death, flogging and whipping, penalties prescribed by Iranian law for adultery, must be considered forms of prohibited treatment under Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court recognized these punishments as prohibited treatment under Article 3.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that Turkey had availed itself of the geographic preference option under the Geneva Convention to give preference to asylum-seekers from European countries and that the applicant failed to comply with the five-day requirement under the 1994 Asylum Regulation, so temporary residence permits could not be extended to her.

anchor.surface_text: The Government maintained in reply that when becoming a Contracting Party to the 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees ("the Geneva Convention"), Turkey had availed itself of the geographic preference option in the Convention to give preference to asylum-seekers from European countries (see paragraph 26 above). However, for humanitarian reasons the authorities issue temporary residence permits to non-European asylum-seekers like the applicant who are recognised as refugees by the UNHCR pending their resettlement in a third country. Given that the applicant failed to comply with the five-day requirement under the 1994 Asylum Regulation (see paragraphs 27-28 above), this facility could not be extended to her.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the automatic and mechanical application of the five-day time-limit incompatible with Article 3 protection and that the applicant was denied meaningful assessment.

arguments.claim: The Government questioned the substance of the applicant’s fears, noting her failure to apply for asylum on arrival in Turkey and Paris, doubting whether she would have sought refugee status if she had entered Canada.

anchor.surface_text: The Government further questioned the substance of the applicant’s fears. In their opinion the fact that the applicant failed to make an application to the authorities or to the UNHCR when she arrived in Turkey in 1997 was at variance with her allegations under Article 3 of the Convention. It was also significant that she did not claim asylum status when she arrived at the airport in Paris (see paragraph 14 above). In the Government’s view, it must be doubted whether the applicant would ever have sought refugee status if she had managed to enter Canada.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court was not persuaded by the Government's doubts and gave weight to the UNHCR's findings and reports on Iran.

arguments.claim: Contracting States have the right to control entry, residence and expulsion of aliens, and the right to political asylum is not contained in the Convention or its Protocols.

anchor.surface_text: the right to political asylum is not contained in either the Convention or its Protocols (see the Vilvarajah and Others v. the United Kingdom judgment of 30 October 1991, Series A no. 215, p. 34, § 102). However, it is well established in the case-law of the Court that expulsion by a Contracting State may give rise to an issue under Article 3, and hence engage the responsibility of that State under the Convention, where substantial grounds have been shown for believing that the person in question, if expelled, would face a real risk of being subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 in the receiving country.

arguments.claim: Article 3 implies the obligation not to expel a person to a country where there is a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3, as established in Soering, Cruz Varas, and Chahal judgments.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 implies the obligation not to expel the person in question to that country (see the Soering v. the United Kingdom judgment of 7 July 1989, Series A no. 161, pp. 35-36, §§ 90-91; the Cruz Varas and Others v. Sweden judgment of 20 March 1991, Series A no. 201, p. 28, §§ 69-70; and the Chahal v. the United Kingdom judgment of 15 November 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V, p. 1853, §§ 73-74).

arguments.claim: A rigorous scrutiny must be conducted of an individual’s claim that deportation will expose them to treatment prohibited by Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: a rigorous scrutiny must necessarily be conducted of an individual’s claim that his or her deportation to a third country will expose that individual to treatment prohibited by Article 3 (see, mutatis mutandis, the Chahal judgment cited above, p. 1855, § 79, and p. 1859, § 96).

arguments.claim: The authorities of the respondent State did not conduct any meaningful assessment of the applicant’s claim, and the five-day registration requirement denied her scrutiny of the factual basis of her fears.

anchor.surface_text: The Court is not persuaded that the authorities of the respondent State conducted any meaningful assessment of the applicant’s claim, including its arguability. It would appear that the applicant’s failure to comply with the five-day registration requirement under the Asylum Regulation 1994 denied her any scrutiny of the factual basis of her fears about being removed to Iran (see paragraph 16 above).

arguments.claim: The automatic and mechanical application of the five-day time-limit for submitting an asylum application is at variance with the protection of the fundamental value embodied in Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: In the Court’s opinion, the automatic and mechanical application of such a short time-limit for submitting an asylum application must be considered at variance with the protection of the fundamental value embodied in Article 3 of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The Ankara Administrative Court limited itself to the formal legality of the deportation rather than the substance of the applicant’s fears, despite the applicant having more than an arguable claim of risk.

anchor.surface_text: The Ankara Administrative Court, on her application for judicial review, limited itself to the issue of the formal legality of the applicant’s deportation rather than the more compelling question of the substance of her fears, even though by that stage the applicant must be considered to have had more than an arguable claim that she would be at risk if removed to her country of origin.

arguments.claim: The Court must give due weight to the UNHCR’s conclusion on the applicant’s claim in assessing the risk faced if deported.

anchor.surface_text: The Court for its part must give due weight to the UNHCR’s conclusion on the applicant’s claim in making its own assessment of the risk which the applicant would face if her deportation were to be implemented.

arguments.claim: The Government have not disputed the applicant’s reliance on Amnesty International findings concerning punishments for adultery in Iran.

anchor.surface_text: It is further to be observed that the Government have not sought to dispute the applicant’s reliance on the findings of Amnesty International concerning the punishment meted out to women who are found guilty of adultery (see paragraph 34 above).

arguments.claim: The situation in Iran has not evolved to the extent that adulterous behaviour is no longer considered reprehensible; stoning remains on the statute book and may be resorted to by authorities.

anchor.surface_text: the Court is not persuaded that the situation in the applicant’s country of origin has evolved to the extent that adulterous behaviour is no longer considered a reprehensible affront to Islamic law. It has taken judicial notice of recent surveys of the current situation in Iran and notes that punishment of adultery by stoning still remains on the statute book and may be resorted to by the authorities (see paragraphs 31-32 above).

arguments.claim: There is a real risk of the applicant being subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 if returned to Iran; deportation would violate Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: Having regard to the above considerations, the Court finds it substantiated that there is a real risk of the applicant being subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 if she were to be returned to Iran. Accordingly, the order for her deportation to Iran would, if executed, give rise to a violation of Article 3.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the risk substantiated and that deportation would violate Article 3.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained she did not have an effective remedy to challenge the rejection of her asylum application as out of time, breaching Article 13.

anchor.surface_text: Articles 3 and 13 of the Convention in respect of these two complaints.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found a violation of Article 13 due to lack of effective remedy.

arguments.claim: The applicant maintained that since her asylum application was out of time she was never afforded an opportunity to explain her fear of deportation; no appeal existed against rejection; judicial review could not suspend deportation or examine merits.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant maintained that since her application for asylum was out of time she was never afforded an opportunity to explain to the authorities why she feared deportation to Iran. There was no appeal against the rejection of her asylum application. Furthermore, her action before the Ankara Administrative Court could not be considered an effective remedy since that court could not suspend the deportation decision with immediate effect. The court did not give detailed reasons for its decision not to suspend the applicant’s deportation since the decision was an interim one and a separate decision would have been required.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court agreed that the remedy was ineffective as it lacked suspension and merits examination.

arguments.claim: The Government acknowledged the Ankara Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s request for suspension and annulment of deportation but argued she failed to request annulment of the asylum rejection; the court was bound to dismiss since no deportation order had been made.

anchor.surface_text: The Government acknowledged that the Ankara Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s request for suspension and annulment of the deportation order. However, she failed to request the annulment of the decision rejecting her asylum request. The Ankara Administrative Court was bound to dismiss the applicant’s request with regard to her deportation since no such order had as yet been made.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the remedy was ineffective despite the Government's procedural argument.

arguments.claim: Domestic courts can stay execution of administrative acts if irreversible harm would be caused and the act is clearly unlawful; appeal lies to the Supreme Administrative Court.

anchor.surface_text: With reference to the provisions of Article 125 of the Constitution (see paragraph 22 above), the Government maintained that the domestic courts are empowered to stay the execution of an administrative act if irreversible harm would be caused to a plaintiff and the act is clearly unlawful. Furthermore, an appeal from the decision of an administrative court lies to the Supreme Administrative Court (see paragraph 25 above).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the judicial review proceedings did not provide the required safeguards under Article 13.

arguments.claim: The Government contended the applicant had an effective remedy to challenge her deportation.

anchor.surface_text: For these reasons, the Government contended that the applicant had an effective remedy to challenge her deportation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded the judicial review proceedings did not satisfy Article 13 requirements.

arguments.claim: Article 13 requires a domestic remedy to enforce the substance of Convention rights and grant appropriate relief, with some discretion to States on how to conform.

anchor.surface_text: The Court recalls that Article 13 guarantees the availability at national level of a remedy to enforce the substance of the Convention rights and freedoms in whatever form they might happen to be secured in the domestic legal order. The effect of this Article is thus to require the provision of a domestic remedy allowing the competent national authority both to deal with the substance of the relevant Convention complaint and to grant appropriate relief, although Contracting States are afforded some discretion as to the manner in which they conform to their obligations under this provision.

arguments.claim: The aggregate of remedies provided by national law may satisfy Article 13 in certain circumstances.

anchor.surface_text: Moreover, in certain circumstances the aggregate of remedies provided by national law may satisfy the requirements of Article 13 (see the Chahal judgment cited above, pp. 1869-70, § 145).

arguments.claim: There was no assessment by domestic authorities of the applicant’s risk claim; refusal to consider asylum request for procedural reasons could not be appealed; judicial review did not allow suspension or merits examination.

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that there was no assessment made by the domestic authorities of the applicant’s claim to be at risk if removed to Iran. The refusal to consider her asylum request for non-respect of procedural requirements could not be taken on appeal. Admittedly the applicant was able to challenge the legality of her deportation in judicial review proceedings. However, this course of action entitled her neither to suspend its implementation nor to have an examination of the merits of her claim to be at risk.

arguments.claim: The Ankara Administrative Court considered the deportation fully in line with domestic law and felt no need to address the substance of the complaint, despite the claim being arguable on the merits.

anchor.surface_text: The Ankara Administrative Court considered that the applicant’s deportation was fully in line with domestic law requirements. It would appear that, having reached that conclusion, the court felt it unnecessary to address the substance of the applicant’s complaint, even though it was arguable on the merits in view of the UNHCR’s decision to recognise her as a refugee within the meaning of the Geneva Convention.

arguments.claim: Given the irreversible harm that might occur and the importance of Article 3, an effective remedy under Article 13 requires independent and rigorous scrutiny of claims and possibility of suspending implementation.

anchor.surface_text: In the Court’s opinion, given the irreversible nature of the harm that might occur if the risk of torture or ill-treatment alleged materialised and the importance which it attaches to Article 3, the notion of an effective remedy under Article 13 requires independent and rigorous scrutiny of a claim that there exist substantial grounds for fearing a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 and the possibility of suspending the implementation of the measure impugned.

arguments.claim: Since the Ankara Administrative Court failed to provide these safeguards, the judicial review proceedings did not satisfy Article 13 requirements.

anchor.surface_text: Since the Ankara Administrative Court failed in the circumstances to provide any of these safeguards, the Court is led to conclude that the judicial review proceedings relied on by the Government did not satisfy the requirements of Article 13.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court concluded there was a violation of Article 13 due to ineffective remedy.
